tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

1	# Kitty: shared trip costs — design
2	
3	Date: 2026-11-17
4	
5	## Intent
6	
7	A small command-line tool for a group of friends on a trip to record who paid
8	for what, and at the end see who owes whom. The owner is not a programmer;
9	their friend Sam writes scripts and will connect the tool's output to a
10	spreadsheet. So every report prints machine-readable JSON, and the expenses can
11	be exported to CSV.
12	
13	Success: during the trip people add expenses and repayments with short commands,
14	`balances` / `settle` give correct, predictable numbers that agree to the cent,
15	and Sam's scripts can read everything without special cases.
16	
17	## Goals
18	
19	- All of Sam's commands (below), with his exact output shapes.
20	- Money is exact: whole cents, never floating point. Shares of an expense always
21	  add up exactly to the expense's converted amount.
22	- Bad input gives a clear message and stops with exit status 1. Never a Python
23	  traceback.
24	
25	## Non-goals
26	
27	- No editing of an expense (remove and re-add instead).
28	- No listing or removing of payments (not in Sam's list; see "Calls to check").
29	- No multiple kitties per folder, no sync, no undo, no interactive prompts.
30	
31	## Anti-goals
32	
33	- Old numbers silently changing: a later rate change or a new member must never
34	  alter an expense that is already recorded.
35	- Rounding that is unpredictable or doesn't add up.
36	- Anything that needs installing beyond the Python already on the Mac.
37	
38	## Constraints
39	
40	- Runs with the system Python on the owner's Mac: **Python 3.9.6**. Standard
41	  library only. Must not use 3.10+ syntax (`match`, `X | Y` in runtime
42	  annotations, etc.).
43	- Invoked as `python3 -m kitty <command> ...` from the folder containing the
44	  `kitty` package.
45	- State lives in `kitty.json` in the **current working directory**.
46	
47	## Approaches considered
48	
49	- **A. Small package of a few modules plus automated tests (chosen).** Storage,
50	  money/splitting math, the ledger logic, and the command-line layer are
51	  separate, with tests using the built-in `unittest`. Lets the rounding rules and
52	  error cases be verified, and Sam can find things easily later.
53	- **B. One single file.** Easier to glance at, but harder to test piece by piece
54	  and gets tangled as it grows.
55	
56	The owner handed over the technical side; A was chosen by the designer.
57	
58	## Decisions made with the owner
59	
60	### Group membership
61	
62	- An expense split "between everyone" means **the members at the moment the
63	  expense is added**. The split is stored with the expense; people who join
64	  later are not in it.
65	- `member remove NAME` **refuses** if NAME appears in any expense or payment at
66	  all — as payer, as someone with a share (even a 0.00 share), or as sender or
67	  receiver of a payment — even if their balance is zero. If they appear nowhere,
68	  they are removed.
69	
70	### Exchange rates
71	
72	- `rate set CUR R` means 1 CUR = R main-currency units, from now on.
73	- Each expense and payment stores the rate it was converted with. Changing a
74	  rate later never changes anything already recorded.
75	- Setting a rate for the main currency is refused as a mistake.
76	- Using a currency with no rate set is refused (message says to `rate set` it
77	  first).
78	- Conversion: `amount × rate`, rounded to the cent, **halves up**
79	  (0.125 → 0.13). Use `decimal.Decimal` with `ROUND_HALF_UP`.
80	
81	### Splitting (the owner's family rule)
82	
83	All splitting happens in **cents of the main currency, after conversion**:
84	
85	1. Convert the expense to main-currency cents `T` (as above).
86	2. Give each person a weight: equal split → 1 each; `--shares` → their share;
87	   `--percent` → their percent; `--exact` → their exact amount.
88	3. Each person gets `floor(T × weight / total_weight)` cents (exact rational
89	   arithmetic, e.g. `fractions.Fraction` or integer math — never floats).
90	4. The leftover cents (always fewer than the number of people) go **one each to
91	   people in order, starting from the first**. Size of the leftover fraction
92	   does not matter.
93	
94	Order is the order the names were typed in `--among`, `--exact`, `--shares`,
95	`--percent`; for a split between everyone, the order people joined the group.
96	
97	Worked examples (must be tests):
98	
99	- €10.00 between Alice, Bob, Cara → 3.34, 3.33, 3.33.
100	- €10.00 with `--shares A=1,B=2` → A 3.34, B 6.66 (not 3.33 / 6.67).
101	- Percentages work the same way as shares.
102	
103	Validation:
104	
105	- `--exact` amounts are in the **expense's own currency** and must add up
106	  **exactly** to the expense amount, or it refuses (no auto-fixing). For a
107	  main-currency expense the shares are then exactly those amounts; for a foreign
108	  one they are proportions of the converted total via the rule above.
109	- `--percent` values must add up to **exactly 100**, or it refuses.
110	
111	## Commands and behaviour
112	
113	General rules (designer's calls unless noted):
114	
115	- Every command except `init` needs an existing `kitty.json`; otherwise error
116	  "no kitty here, run init first".
117	- On success, commands that change things print nothing, except `expense add`,
118	  which prints the new ID as a bare number (e.g. `1`). Reports print one line of
119	  JSON to stdout, using `json.dumps` default separators (matches Sam's examples)
120	  with `ensure_ascii=False` so names like "Zoë" print as typed.
121	- Errors: `error: <message>` on stderr, exit status 1. This includes argument
122	  parsing mistakes (override argparse's default exit status 2) and an unreadable
123	  or corrupt `kitty.json`.
124	- Money in output: a string with exactly two decimals, e.g. `"20.70"`,
125	  `"-20.70"`, `"0.00"`. Main currency everywhere, except an expense's own
126	  `amount`.
127	- Saving is atomic (write a temp file in the same folder, then rename) so a
128	  crash can't leave a half-written `kitty.json`.
129	
130	Input rules:
131	
132	- **Currency codes:** three letters, converted to uppercase (`usd` → `USD`).
133	- **Names:** case-sensitive, non-empty, may not contain `,` or `=` (they're the
134	  separators in the split options). Duplicate names refused. Every name used
135	  anywhere must be a current member.
136	- **Amounts** (expense, payment, exact parts): positive, at most two decimals,
137	  plain digits (`45`, `45.5`, `45.00`). Reject zero, negatives, `1e3`, `nan`,
138	  `inf`, non-numbers.
139	- **Rates:** positive decimal, any number of decimal places, plain digits.
140	- **Shares / percents:** positive decimals (e.g. `1.5`, `33.5`).
141	- **Split option lists** (`A=30,B=20` / `A,B`): each name at most once; at most
142	  one of `--among`, `--exact`, `--shares`, `--percent` per expense.
143	- **Dates:** a real calendar date in `YYYY-MM-DD`; default today (local time).
144	
145	### `init CUR`
146	
147	Creates `kitty.json` with main currency CUR. Refuses if `kitty.json` already
148	exists (so a trip can't be wiped by accident).
149	
150	### `member add NAME` / `member remove NAME` / `member list`
151	
152	`list` prints names in join order: `["Alice", "Bob"]`. Removal rule above.
153	A removed member who is added again goes to the end of the order.
154	
155	### `expense add PAYER AMOUNT DESCRIPTION [options]`
156	
157	- DESCRIPTION is the remaining words joined with single spaces (so quoting is
158	  optional); must not be empty. Options may come before or after it.
159	- Options: `--among`, `--exact`, `--shares`, `--percent`, `--currency`
160	  (default main), `--date` (default today), `--category` (default `other`,
161	  stored as typed).
162	- The payer doesn't have to be among the people sharing.
163	- IDs are 1, 2, 3, … and never reused after removal (store the next ID).
164	- Stored per expense: id, date, payer, description, amount (cents, own
165	  currency), currency, rate used, base_amount (cents), category, and the shares
166	  as an ordered list of (name, cents).
167	
168	### `expense list` / `expense remove ID`
169	
170	`list` in ID order, exactly Sam's shape:

tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## When to use

A fresh agent costs more than it looks. It knows only what you put in the prompt, and you see only the summary it sends back — both handoffs drop detail, and neither of you can tell what the other missed. You can't watch it work, only wait or cancel. Its mistakes come back in the same confident register as its findings, and an agent handed your hypothesis tends to return it confirmed. Several at once spend tokens in a burst the user didn't ask for. Weigh those tokens against the accuracy they buy: the user pays for agents you did not need, and pays again for work you redo because you skipped one.

Reach for this when you have independent work to run in parallel, when the user asks for a side quest that shouldn't block your main thread, or when answering would mean reading across several files — delegate that and you keep the conclusion, not the file dumps.

Do the work yourself when it is a handful of tool calls or a lookup whose target you already know; don't delegate a check you could run inline. Delegate review only when you want a read that isn't anchored on yours — then give it the code, not your conclusion. Once you've delegated something, don't also run it yourself; wait for the result. When in doubt, don't spawn.

When you do spawn one, brief it like the peer it is: state the goal and what you have already ruled out, point it at the files and docs worth reading instead of retyping them, and keep the scope explicit and narrow. That brief is the only context it will have, so it is your first lever on every cost above — and if you cannot write a clear one, you do not understand the task well enough to hand it off.

A fork keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.
